newsitem.title: INDIA: India must allow free rein to broadcasters - U.S..
newsitem.headline: India must allow free rein to broadcasters - U.S..

text.p: U.S. Federal Communication Commission (FCC) chairman Reed Hundt urged India on Wednesday to design a broadcasting regulatory structure which provides views from a diverse range of independent sources.
Hundt, on a visit to India, said broadcasting can nurture the diversity and vibracy of India's society.
"But broadcasting will be most effective if the energy and creativity of content providers, both Indian and international, is given the freest possible rein to flourish," he said in a statement.
He said this did not imply anarchy or absence of regulation.
"It means a regulatory structure designed to provide viewers and listeners with a diverse range of programming from many independent sources," the U.S. regulator said.
The FCC is an independent agency responsible for regulating both broadcasting and telecommunications in the United States.
India, which began opening up key sectors under an economic liberalisation programme launched in 1991, is overhauling its domestic broadcast laws.

Indian Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy on Tuesday said a domestic broadcast regulator will be set up under a planned law to free up the air waves having powers to enforce competition.

In May, Reddy introduced in parliament a draft of the Broadcast Bill and sent it to a multi-party committee of lawmakers who are examining the bill amid intense lobbying by foreign and domestic broadcasters.
The bill is expected to be put to a vote in parliament later this year after the committee proposes changes.

In India, the state still owns radio and television stations that broadcast from India, and there has been strong opposition to opening up broadcast media to the private sector, particularly foreign broadcasters.
The government leases out time-slots to private producers, but news programmes are subject to restrictions.

Dozens of time-slots are available to private producers with stipulated proportions of advertising time, but they cannot set up their own stations to air their programmes or acquire broadcast frequencies.

Hundt said that in the future, the distinction between broadcasting and telecom services may be blurred, and it would be helpful to have a single regulatory agency dealing with both categories of service.
"It is also important that the regulatory structure or structures be transparent," he said.

"In order to provide service providers with the right incentives, they need to know the rules of the game, to be able to participate in regulatory proceedings and to understand the basis for regulators' decisions," he said.
